nameStory: The Snow Goose gets its name from its brilliant white plumage that looks like fresh snow against the sky. When thousands of these birds take flight together during migration, they create a swirling blizzard of white wings that early observers compared to a snowstorm in motion.
description: Snow Geese are large, stocky waterfowl about the size of a Canada Goose, with bright white bodies and black wingtips. They have thick orange bills and orange legs that look almost carrot-colored. Interestingly, some Snow Geese come in a dark 'blue' morph with a white head and dark blue-gray body, though the white form is much more common in New England.

idTips.label: White plumage with black wingtips
idTips.description: Brilliant white body with jet-black wingtips that are most visible in flight, creating a stark contrast like a white sheet with black trim

idTips.label: Orange bill and legs
idTips.description: Thick, carrot-orange bill with a distinctive black 'grinning patch' along the edges, and matching orange-pink legs

idTips.label: Stocky build
idTips.description: Robust, barrel-shaped body that looks compact and sturdy, with a relatively short neck compared to swans

idTips.label: Loud honking calls
idTips.description: High-pitched, nasal honking that sounds like a rusty gate or old car horn, often heard before you see the birds

idTips.label: V-formation flight
idTips.description: Fly in classic V-formations or long diagonal lines, with steady wingbeats and necks extended straight forward

habitat: Snow Geese visit New England's coastal areas, large lakes, and flooded agricultural fields during migration. Look for them in salt marshes, tidal flats, and shallow ponds along the coast, as well as in corn and grain fields inland where they stop to feed.

seasonality.spring: Peak migration occurs in March and April, with large flocks moving north to Arctic breeding grounds. Listen for their distinctive calls overhead and scan coastal areas and farm fields.
seasonality.summer: Very rare in summer as they breed far north in the Arctic tundra. Any summer sightings are likely injured birds or stragglers.
seasonality.fall: Return migration brings flocks through New England from October through December. This is often the best time to see large numbers feeding in agricultural areas.
seasonality.winter: Small numbers may winter along the coast, especially in milder years. Check coastal marshes and ice-free waters for overwintering birds.

funFact: Snow Geese can live over 25 years and return to the exact same nesting area where they were born, navigating thousands of miles using the Earth's magnetic field, star patterns, and even infrasound from ocean waves that humans can't hear.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with Tundra Swans, but Snow Geese are smaller with shorter necks, orange bills (not yellow and black), and black wingtips. Memory trick: 'Snow Geese have orange beaks like carrots in the snow.'
contextualKnowledge: The 'Blue Goose' was once thought to be a separate species until scientists discovered it was just a color variation of the Snow Goose. Both white and blue forms can appear in the same family, and they interbreed freely, sometimes producing birds with mixed coloring.
compareHints: Unlike the Greater White-fronted Goose which has a white forehead patch and orange legs, Snow Geese are predominantly white all over with black wingtips. Ross's Geese are very similar but smaller with shorter, more triangular bills lacking the black 'grinning patch.' Greylag Geese are much grayer overall with pink bills rather than the Snow Goose's brilliant white plumage and orange bill.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the grey geese in its genus, Greylag Geese lack the white forehead patch of Greater White-fronted Geese and aren't pure white like Snow Geese.
Unlike Snow Geese which are mostly white or very pale, Greater White-fronted Geese are brown and gray with distinctive belly markings.
Among the grey geese, Pink-footed Geese are smaller and more compact than Greylag Geese, lack the white forehead of Greater White-fronted Geese, and have much pinker legs than any of their relatives.
Compared to Snow Geese in the same genus, Ross's Geese are significantly smaller with proportionally smaller, cleaner bills lacking black edges.
Among grey geese, Swan Goose is unmistakable due to its exceptionally long neck and orange bill.
Compared to other grey geese in its genus, Tundra Bean Goose lacks the white forehead patch of Greater White-fronted Goose and the distinctive bill pattern of Pink-footed Goose.
